fenced.name: New International Version
fenced.publisher: Zondervan, part of HarperCollins, a News Corp company
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without asking — provided it isn't a complete book of the Bible and isn't 25% or more of your work. Past that: written permission.

fenced.name: English Standard Version
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without a license — not more than half of any one book, not 25% or more of your work. The ESV may not be published under a Creative Commons license.

fenced.name: New Revised Standard Version (and NRSVue)
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses free — under 25% of your work's words, text unaltered, notice included. Past that: written approval.

fenced.name: New American Standard Bible
fenced.policy: Quote up to 1,000 verses without permission — not a complete book, not more than 50% of your work.

fenced.name: New Living Translation
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without permission — not a complete book, not more than 25% of your work.

fenced.name: Christian Standard Bible
fenced.policy: Quote up to 1,000 verses without permission — not a complete book, not more than 50% of your work.

fenced.name: Revised Standard Version
fenced.policy: Still under copyright and actively licensed, seventy years on. On the standard 95-year US term, the 1952 text enters the public domain in 2048.

fenced.name: New King James Version
fenced.owner: Thomas Nelson, part of HarperCollins Christian Publishing
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without written permission — not more than 25% of your work, not more than 50% of any one book of the Bible, and not in a commentary or other Bible reference work.

fenced.name: Good News Translation (Today's English Version, Second Edition)
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without written permission — not 50% of a complete book of the Bible, not 25% or more of your work.

fenced.name: The Message
fenced.publisher: NavPress, represented by Tyndale House Publishers
fenced.policy: Quote up to 500 verses without written permission — not a complete book of the Bible, not 25% or more of your work.

fenced.name: New American Bible, Revised Edition
fenced.owner: Confraternity of Christian Doctrine, Washington, D.C.
fenced.publisher: permissions through the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops
fenced.policy: Quote fewer than 5,000 words without permission — under 40% of any one book of the Bible and under 40% of your work. Complete books may not be podcast; apps, paid or free, need a license.

fenced.name: Common English Bible
fenced.policy: Quote under 500 verses without permission — not an entire book of the Bible, not 25% or more of your work. Past that, a fee is assessed.

fenced.name: Legacy Standard Bible
fenced.publisher: managed in partnership with Three Sixteen Publishing
fenced.policy: Quote up to 1,000 verses without written permission — not a complete book, not more than 50% of your work, and no more than 1,000 verses in an electronic retrieval system. Named AI systems may quote up to 1,000 verses in one response.

free.name: King James Version
free.note: Free in America. In the United Kingdom, though, it is still printed under perpetual Royal Letters Patent — only Cambridge, Oxford, and the Crown's licensees may print it there. The oldest fence of all belongs to the Crown.

life.note: public domain by age (in the US)

free.name: American Standard Version
free.note: One of the first copyrighted English Bibles — its 1901 title page states the reason: “to insure purity of text.” The copyright expired in 1957, and the text has been free ever since.

free.name: World English Bible
free.note: A modern revision of the ASV, dedicated entirely to the public domain — the name is trademarked, the text is free. It is the translation this site quotes most.

free.name: Berean Standard Bible
free.note: Released into the public domain on April 30, 2023 — a complete modern translation, given away whole.

free.name: Open English Bible
free.note: Published under a Creative Commons Zero dedication: no rights reserved, anywhere, for anything.

free.name: NET Bible
free.note: Copyrighted by Biblical Studies Press, but deliberately open: quote it in any form for non-commercial use without asking, and download the full text free. “Ministry first” is their stated policy.

free.name: Douay-Rheims (Challoner)
free.note: The historic English Bible of Catholics, in Challoner's revision — free for centuries.

free.name: Brenton's English Septuagint
free.note: Sir Lancelot Brenton's English translation of the Greek Old Testament — published in 1851, free by age, and the Septuagint column in this site's polyglot.

free.name: R. H. Charles: 1 Enoch and Jubilees
free.note: Charles's translations of 1 Enoch and Jubilees from the Oxford pseudepigrapha volumes — published before 1931, so free in the United States and nearly everywhere else.

free.name: Lexham English Bible
free.note: Copyrighted by Lexham Press, but anyone may give it away whole — just not sell it on its own. Under 100 verses, a plain (LEB) tag is enough; more than that, the full credit line. A middle way between the fence and the gift.

life.note: copyrighted but free to give away

story.title: The King’s Bible
story.note: The Authorized Version is printed under royal privilege. In England, the right to print it belongs to the Crown to this day.

story.title: The first fence
story.note: The American Standard Version is copyrighted by Thomas Nelson & Sons — the title page gives the reason: “to insure purity of text.” Protection, not profit, was the stated motive.

story.title: The churches take the copyright
story.note: The Revised Standard Version is published and owned by the National Council of Churches — a council of churches becomes a Bible rights-holder. The RSV is still under copyright today.

story.title: The bestseller era
story.note: The complete NIV appears. Biblica owns it; Zondervan sells it; it becomes the best-selling modern English Bible in the world.

story.title: The fences multiply
story.note: NKJV (1982), NRSV (1989), NLT (1996), ESV (2001), The Message (2002), CEB (2011), CSB (2017), LSB (2021) — nearly every major modern translation is proprietary, each with its own quotation allowance and its own permission desk.

story.title: The gift returns
story.note: The World English Bible is dedicated to the public domain; the Open English Bible follows under CC0. Modern translations, freely given.

story.title: Given away whole
story.note: The Berean Standard Bible enters the public domain on April 30, 2023 — proof that it can still be done.
